Fréquence = 1 ÷ période, et longueur d'o: Frequency = 1 ÷ period, and wavelength = speed ÷ frequency.
Le son est une onde de pression, pas de: Sound is a pressure wave, no sound in a vacuum. 343 m/s in air: 3 seconds per kilometre.
Une corde pincée, une membrane de haut-p: A plucked string, a loudspeaker cone or your vocal cords push the air, which compresses, then relaxes. This compression is passed along step by step, like a push in a queue of people: it is a pressure wave. The air does not travel, only the push moves forward. Without matter there is nothing to push: sound does not cross a vacuum.
Fréquence = hauteur, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitud: Frequency = pitch, f = 1 ÷ T. Amplitude = loudness. λ = v ÷ f: A 440 Hz is 0.78 m long.
La fréquence f, en hertz, compte les vib: Frequency f, in hertz, counts the vibrations per second; it gives the pitch. The higher it is, the higher the sound. It is the inverse of the period T, the duration of one vibration: f = 1 ÷ T. For a period of 0.002 s, f = 1 ÷ 0.002 = 500 Hz. The tuning fork, invented in 1711 by John Shore, trumpeter at the English court, vibrates 440 times a second: that is the A.
L'amplitude, elle, donne l'intensité, me: Amplitude gives the intensity, measured in decibels. The two are independent: a low A can be very loud, a high A very soft. And the wave has a length: the distance covered during one vibration, λ = v ÷ f. For A at 440 Hz in air: λ = 343 ÷ 440 ≈ 0.78 m. Bass notes have wavelengths of several metres, hence big loudspeakers.
Hertz : ondes radio (fin des années 1880: Hertz: radio waves (late 1880s). Light arrives at once, sound takes its time.
L'unité de fréquence porte le nom de Hei: The unit of frequency is named after Heinrich Hertz, who demonstrated radio waves at the end of the 1880s. Yet they are waves very different from sound: electromagnetic, they cross the vacuum at the speed of light. Sound needs air, water or a solid. The same word, "wave", covers both because they obey the same vibration equations.
C'est pourquoi on voit l'éclair avant d': That is why you see the lightning before hearing the thunder: they are born at the same moment, but the light arrives almost at once while the sound takes its time. A 1,000 Hz sound vibrates five times faster than a 200 Hz sound: it sounds more than two octaves higher.

La portée a cinq lignes et se lit comme: The staff has five lines and reads like a graph: time runs from left to right, high notes at the top, low at the bottom. Around 1030 Guido of Arezzo had the idea of taking the first syllable of each line of the Latin hymn to Saint John the Baptist, Ut queant laxis, each line of which starts one step higher: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la. Ut would later become do, easier to sing.

Un point juste après une note ajoute la: A dot just after a note adds half its value. A dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = 3 quarter notes; a dotted quarter note, one and a half quarters, that is 3 eighth notes. Careful: a dot above or below the note is something else, it asks for it to be played detached.
Haut : nombre de temps. Bas : quelle fig: Top: number of beats. Bottom: which note is one beat. 3/4 = the waltz. Petrucci (1501): printed music.
La mesure regroupe les temps. Le chiffre: The time signature groups the beats. The top number counts the beats; the bottom one says which note value is one beat: 4 for the quarter note, 8 for the eighth. In 4/4, four quarter notes per bar, the most common time. In 3/4, three quarter notes: that is the waltz, first beat stressed, oom, pah, pah.
Pendant des siècles, la musique se copia: For centuries music was copied by hand. In 1501 in Venice, Ottaviano Petrucci published the Harmonice Musices Odhecaton, the first collection of polyphonic music printed with movable type: notes, staves and words went under the press in several passes. The score became an object that travels.
Octave = fréquence × 2, corde ÷ 2 (Philo: Octave = frequency × 2, string ÷ 2 (Philolaus). A 440 Hz: London 1939, ISO 16 standard.
Monter d'une octave, c'est doubler la fr: Going up an octave means doubling the frequency: f = 2 × 440 = 880 Hz for the A above. The two notes blend so well that they get the same name. On a string it is half: a string half as long vibrates twice as fast. In the 5th century BC the Pythagorean Philolaus already linked the octave to the ratio 2/1.
Le la de référence à 440 Hz a été recomm: The reference A at 440 Hz was recommended in London in 1939, then adopted by the ISO 16 standard. Before that it varied from city to city: France had set its own at 435 Hz in the mid-19th century. A touring orchestra could find itself out of tune with the local organ.
Quinte 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), quarte 4/3, t: Fifth 3/2 (440 → 660 Hz), fourth 4/3, third 5/4. Pythagoras' hammers: a legend.
Après l'octave, l'intervalle le plus sim: After the octave, the simplest interval is the perfect fifth, at ratio 3/2: on a string, two thirds of the length. Above an A at 440 Hz, the fifth vibrates at f = 440 × 3/2 = 660 Hz. Next come the fourth, 4/3, and the natural major third, 5/4. Philolaus already gave the fifth the ratio 3/2.
La légende veut que Pythagore ait découv: Legend has it that Pythagoras discovered these ratios by listening to blacksmiths' hammers of different weights. Nicomachus of Gerasa and then Boethius tell it. It is physically false: a hammer's note does not follow its weight the way a string's follows its length. The ratios themselves are true, and can be checked on a string.
12 demi-tons par octave, un ton = 2 demi: 12 semitones per octave, a tone = 2 semitones, fifth = 7. Sharp raises, flat lowers, natural cancels.
L'octave occidentale compte 12 demi-tons: The Western octave has 12 semitones: on a piano, seven white keys and five black before you reach the same note again. A tone is two semitones: from C to D you pass through C♯. The perfect fifth has seven: C, C♯, D, D♯, E, F, F♯, G.
Le dièse (♯) monte une note d'un demi-to: The sharp (♯) raises a note by a semitone, the flat (♭) lowers it by a semitone, and the natural (♮) cancels both. On a piano C♯ and D♭ fall on the same black key; on a violin a player may play them very slightly differently.

La gamme majeure suit toujours le même m: The major scale always follows the same pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone, tone, semitone. Start from C and you get C D E F G A B C, on the white keys alone: the semitones fall between E and F, and between B and C, between the 3rd and 4th notes then the 7th and 8th.
Partez d'une autre note et, pour garder: Start from another note and, to keep the pattern, you need accidentals. From G, the F must go up: G major has an F♯. From F, the B must come down: F major has a B♭. They are written once and for all at the start of the staff: that is the key signature.
La mineur = notes de do majeur, départ e: A minor = notes of C major, starting on A (relative). Pentatonic: 5 notes, the black keys.
La gamme mineure naturelle suit ton, dem: The natural minor scale follows tone, semitone, tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone. Start from A on the white keys and you get it: A minor has exactly the same notes as C major. It is called its relative. Only the tonic, the note of departure and arrival, changes, and with it the whole colour: darker, more melancholy.
Il existe d'autres gammes. La pentatoniq: There are other scales. The pentatonic has only five notes, as its name says: the five black keys of the piano form one. It is found in many of the world's musics, from the blues to traditional songs.
De quinte en quinte, un dièse de plus :: Fifth by fifth, one more sharp: C 0, G 1, D 2. Bach: 24 preludes and fugues per book.
Montez de quinte en quinte depuis do : d: Go up fifth by fifth from C: C, G, D, A… Each major key gains one more sharp. C has none, G has F♯, D has F♯ and C♯, A has three. The other way, going down fifth by fifth, you gain a flat at each step. The twelve keys close up into a circle.
Bach a célébré ce cercle complet. Chaque: Bach celebrated this complete circle. Each book of The Well-Tempered Clavier offers a prelude and fugue in each of the 12 major and 12 minor keys: 24 pairs per book. It still required a keyboard tuning that made all these keys playable.
fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701) : 3e harmoniq: fₙ = n × f (Sauveur, 1701): 3rd harmonic of 110 Hz = 330 Hz. Between 2f and 3f, a hidden fifth.
Une corde ne vibre pas seulement en enti: A string does not vibrate only as a whole. It also vibrates in two halves, three thirds, four quarters, all at once. Each mode gives a frequency: the fundamental f, then the harmonics 2f, 3f, 4f… The n-th harmonic is fₙ = n × f. For a fundamental at 110 Hz, the 3rd harmonic is 3 × 110 = 330 Hz. Joseph Sauveur gave them the name harmonics in 1701.
Sauveur appela aussi « nœuds » les point: Sauveur also called the still points "nodes". A string vibrating in 4 loops at 400 Hz has a fundamental of f = 400 ÷ 4 = 100 Hz. And between the 2nd and 3rd harmonics the ratio is 3f ÷ 2f = 3/2: every note contains a hidden fifth.
Pourquoi une flûte n'est pas un violon: Why a flute is not a violin
Même note, même fondamentale : le timbre: Same note, same fundamental: timbre is the mix of harmonics and the attack. Helmholtz (1863): the resonators.
Une flûte et un violon qui jouent le mêm: A flute and a violin playing the same A have the same fundamental. What sets them apart is timbre: the mix of harmonics, and the way the sound begins, the attack. The violin is rich in harmonics, the flute has few. A pipe open at both ends produces all the harmonics; closed at one end, it favours the odd ones, like the clarinet in its low register, hence its rather hollow tone.
En 1863, Hermann von Helmholtz publie sa: In 1863 Hermann von Helmholtz published his great study of the sensations of tone. To isolate harmonics he used hollow resonators, each tuned to a single frequency, which he held against the ear: you could then hear one harmonic at a time in a sound that seemed single.
Fourier (1822) : tout signal périodique: Fourier (1822): any periodic signal = sum of sine waves. The spectrum analyser shows it.
En 1822, dans sa Théorie analytique de l: In 1822, in his Analytical Theory of Heat, Joseph Fourier showed that a periodic signal, however complicated, can be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves. He was working on heat, not music, but his tool applies to everything that vibrates.
C'est exactement ce que fait un analyseu: That is exactly what a spectrum analyser does: it breaks a sound down into its frequencies and displays the fundamental and its harmonics, each with its own height. Electronic tuners, MP3 compression and song recognition rest on this idea.
Majeur : tierce majeure (4) + mineure (3: Major: major third (4) + minor (3). Minor: the reverse. Rameau (1722): inversions.
L'accord parfait majeur empile deux tier: The major triad stacks two thirds: a major third of 4 semitones, then a minor third of 3. On C: C, E, G, the root, its third and its fifth. The minor triad reverses the order, minor third then major: A, C, E. C minor is formed by lowering the third: C, E♭, G.
En 1722, Jean-Philippe Rameau publie son: In 1722 Jean-Philippe Rameau published his Treatise on Harmony Reduced to its Natural Principles. In it he showed that C-E-G, E-G-C and G-C-E are the same chord, inverted: it takes the name of its root, not of its lowest note. He also set out the fundamental bass, which explains chord progressions.
Rapports simples = consonance (Helmholtz: Simple ratios = consonance (Helmholtz, beats). Zarlino (1558): third 5/4, 264 → 330 Hz.
Les intervalles aux rapports simples son: Intervals with simple ratios sound consonant: the octave 2/1, the fifth 3/2, the major third 5/4, the minor third 6/5. Helmholtz explained it by beats: with a simple ratio few neighbouring harmonics rub against each other; with a complicated ratio they grate.
En 1558, Gioseffo Zarlino défend les tie: In 1558 Gioseffo Zarlino championed pure thirds at ratio 5/4 against the Pythagorean third of 81/64, too wide. The calculation: the natural major third of a C at 264 Hz is f = 264 × 5/4 = 330 Hz. After a perfect cadence, the dominant G resolving onto the tonic C, you hear that the piece is over.
Tonique = repos, dominante = tension. Ca: Tonic = rest, dominant = tension. Perfect cadence: G → C. A chord takes the name of its root.
En harmonie, chaque accord a un rôle dan: In harmony each chord has a role in the key. The tonic, built on the first note, is rest. The dominant, on the fifth, creates a tension that calls for a return. The perfect cadence, dominant then tonic, G then C in C major, has the effect of a full stop.
Les quintes ne retombent pas juste: The fifths do not land true
(3/2)¹² ≈ 129,75 contre 2⁷ = 128 : 1,4 %: (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75 versus 2⁷ = 128: a 1.4 % gap, the Pythagorean comma.
Empilez douze quintes pures depuis un do: Stack twelve pure fifths from a C: you should land on a C seven octaves up. The calculation says no. Twelve fifths are (3/2)¹² ≈ 129.75; seven octaves are 2⁷ = 128. The gap is 129.75 ÷ 128 − 1 ≈ 0.0137, that is 1.4 %. That is the Pythagorean comma, named after Pythagoras because it comes from his tuning by pure fifths.
Conséquence : impossible d'accorder un c: Consequence: you cannot tune a keyboard with all its fifths pure. The error has to be spread somewhere. Meantone temperament, for example, keeps eleven nearly pure fifths and concentrates the error in the twelfth, so grating that it is called the wolf fifth: music that modulated too far became unplayable on a single keyboard.
Demi-ton tempéré = ¹²√2 ≈ 1,0595 (Zhu Za: Tempered semitone = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595 (Zhu Zaiyu, 1584). Fifths barely too small, every key playable.
Le tempérament égal répartit l'erreur pa: Equal temperament spreads the error everywhere: it divides the octave into 12 identical semitones. Twelve semitones must make an octave, so r¹² = 2 and r = ¹²√2 ≈ 1.0595. Each fifth becomes slightly too small, about 1.4983 instead of 1.5, 2 cents less: the ear barely notices. But every key becomes playable.
En 1584, en Chine, le prince Zhu Zaiyu c: In 1584, in China, Prince Zhu Zaiyu calculated the twelfth root of 2 on an abacus to 24 correct decimal places: it was the first exact calculation of this division. In Europe Simon Stevin was working on the same idea at the same time. Almost all pianos are tuned this way today: every interval is slightly off, but all equally so.
Dans les années 1880, Alexander Ellis in: In the 1880s Alexander Ellis invented the cent: one hundredth of a tempered semitone. The octave therefore has 12 × 100 = 1,200. Tuners and music software use it to say how far out a note is: within a few cents, most ears cannot tell the difference.
Et Bach ? Le titre du Clavier bien tempé: And Bach? The title of The Well-Tempered Clavier does not prove he tuned in equal temperament. "Well-tempered" means tuned well enough to play in every key, which other unequal temperaments also allowed. The exact tuning Bach used is still debated.
20 Hz à 20 000 Hz, les aigus partent d'a: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, high frequencies go first. Peak sensitivity around 2,000-5,000 Hz (Fletcher and Munson, 1933).
Une oreille jeune entend de 20 Hz à 20 0: A young ear hears from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below are infrasounds; above, ultrasounds, which bats hear. With age you lose the high frequencies first: that is presbycusis. Nor is the ear equally sensitive everywhere: it is most sensitive around 2,000 to 5,000 Hz, where much of speech intelligibility lies.
En 1933, Harvey Fletcher et Wilden Munso: In 1933 Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson measured it: their curves show that a low sound must be far more intense than a 3,000 Hz sound to seem as loud. That is why the bass seems to disappear when you turn the volume down.
L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀). +10 dB = × 10, +20 dB = × 100, +3 dB ≈ × 2. The bel: Graham Bell.
Cette échelle colle à notre oreille, qui: This scale fits our ear, which perceives ratios rather than differences. But it misleads: two speakers instead of one add only 3 dB, not twice the perceived noise. And with too many decibels, the hair cells of the inner ear are damaged for good.
Frissons musicaux = dopamine (Salimpoor,: Musical chills = dopamine (Salimpoor, 2011). The Mozart effect does not hold. Beethoven deaf, Vienna 1824.
En 2011, Valorie Salimpoor et ses collèg: In 2011 Valorie Salimpoor and her colleagues measured with brain imaging what happens during musical chills: the brain releases dopamine, the same molecule as for food. Music activates the reward circuit, even before the awaited passage: the pleasure of anticipation.
L'« effet Mozart », lui, ne s'est pas co: The "Mozart effect" was not confirmed. The 1993 study described a brief gain on a spatial task; in 1999 a meta-analysis concluded the effect was small, with no change in IQ. And Beethoven composed his Ninth almost totally deaf: at the premiere, in 1824 in Vienna, the singer Caroline Unger had to turn him towards the audience so he could see the applause.
Dans l'air à 20 °C, le son parcourt envi: In air at 20 °C sound travels about 343 m/s; nearly 1,500 m/s in water, and 5,000 to 6,000 m/s in steel. Hence the thunderstorm rule: time equals distance divided by speed, t = d ÷ v. For 1 km: t = 1,000 m ÷ 343 m/s ≈ 2.9 s. Count about 3 seconds between lightning and thunder per kilometre. Newton was the first to calculate the speed of sound. That was in 1687, in the Principia: he found 298 m/s, about 15% too low, because he assumed the air keeps its temperature as it is compressed. Laplace would correct the error.
Les durées se divisent par deux : une ro: Durations are divided by two: a whole note is worth 2 half notes, a half note 2 quarter notes, a quarter note 2 eighth notes. So a whole note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 quarter notes, or 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 eighth notes, and a half note is worth 2 × 2 = 4 eighth notes. The shorter the note, the more beams or flags it gets. The idea that a note's shape sets its duration goes back to Franco of Cologne, in his Ars cantus mensurabilis, around 1250.
Un accord ne prend pas le nom de sa note: A chord takes its name not from its lowest note but from its root: E-G-C is still a C chord. That is Rameau's contribution, which lets you recognise the same function in very different layouts, from a Bach chorale to a pop song. Rameau published this idea in 1722, in his Treatise on Harmony.
Le décibel est logarithmique : L = 10 lo: The decibel is logarithmic: L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀), where I is the intensity and I₀ the threshold of hearing. In practice, +10 dB multiply the intensity by 10. Going from 60 dB to 80 dB is +20 dB, so an intensity multiplied by 10 × 10 = 100. And +3 dB roughly double it, since 10^(3/10) ≈ 2. The bel is named after Alexander Graham Bell; the decibel is a tenth of it. The unit was born in telephony: the Bell System measured its line losses in "transmission units", renamed decibels in 1928.
